questions.question: Describe different types of nanomaterials based on their dimensionality. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe different types of nanomaterials based on their dimensionality.
  • Zero-dimensional (0D): All three dimensions are in the nanoscale (1 –100 nm). Examples: nanoparticles, quantum
  • dots, fullerenes, dendrimers.
  • One-dimensional (1D): Two dimensions are in the nanoscale and one dimension is >100 nm. Examples: carbon
  • nanotubes, nanowires, nanorods, nanofibres.
  • Two-dimensional (2D): One dimension is in the nanoscale and two dimensions are >100 nm. Examples: graphene,
  • graphyne, borophene, phosphorene, nanofilms and nanocoatings.
  • Three-dimensional (3D): All three dimensions are >100 nm, but the material is composed of nanoscale building
  • blocks or possesses nanoscale features. Examples: nanocomposites, nanoparticle disper sions, bundles of
  • nanotubes/nanowires.
  • (Relevant explanation - 4 marks)

questions.question: Recall what carbon dots are. Mention one method of their synthesis and list the raw materials used as carbon sources in their synthesis. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Recall what carbon dots are. Mention one method of their synthesis and list the raw materials used as carbon sources in
  • their synthesis.
  • Carbon dots are quasi spherical nanoparticles primarily made of carbon, however they may also contain hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen
  • or sulphur
  • Hydrothermal method for synthesis of carbon dots: In the hydrothermal method, a carbon-rich precursor such as citric acid or glucose
  • is dissolved in water and sealed in a Teflon-lined autoclave. The mixture is heated at around 150–200 °C for several hours, allowing
  • carbonization and formation of carbon dots. After cooling, the resulting solution is filtered or centrifuged to obtain purifi ed carbon
  • dots.
  • Carbon source: citric acid, glucose, orange peel or any other organic -rich biomass.
  • (Definition of carbon dots – 1 mark, any one method for synthesis of carbon dot – 2 marks, any one carbon source – 1 mark)

questions.question: Describe how magnetic nanoparticles help in enviornmental remediation. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe how magnetic nanoparticles help in environmental remediation.
  • Magnetic nanoparticles play a key role in environmental remediation due to their large surface area, reactivity, and easy mag netic
  • separation. They can adsorb or degrade pollutants such as heavy metals, dyes, and organic contaminants from water and soil.
  • Functionalized magnetic nanoparticles can be tailored with specific coatings to selectively capture target pollutants. After treatment,
  • they can be easily removed from the environment using an external magnetic field, minimizing secondary pollution. Iron ox ide
  • nanoparticles, for example, are widely used to remove arsenic, lead, and chromium from contaminated water. Their reusability and
  • high efficiency make them a sustainable and cost-effective tool for cleaning up environmental pollutants.
  • (Any valid 5 points - 7 marks)

questions.question: Discuss the advantages of nanotechnology-based diagnosis over conventional methods. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the advantages of nanotechnology-based diagnosis over conventional methods.
  • Nanotechnology-based diagnostic methods offer several advantages over conventional approaches. They provide high sensitivity
  • and specificity, allowing detection of minute quantities of biomolecules and enabling early disease diagnosis. The tests are rapid and
  • efficient, significantly reducing the time required for obtaining results. Owing to miniaturization, nanodiagnostic devices are portable
  • and suitable for point-of-care testing. They also allow simultaneous detection of multiple biomarkers, giving a more comprehensive
  • understanding of disease states. Many of these techniques are non -invasive, using samples such as saliva or urine instead of tissue
  • biopsies. Nanoparticles enhance signal generation, leading to greater accuracy and reliability. These system s can also be integrated
  • with digital and smartphone -based platforms for real -time monitoring. Furthermore, they require smaller sample volumes, making
  • them cost-effective, and support personalized medicine by enabling precise biomarker identification for individualized treatment
  • strategies.
  • ( Any valid 5 points - 7 marks)

questions.question: Explain the different types of nanomaterials: (a) carbon-based, (b) metal-based, (c) dendrimers, and (d) composites. Comment on their main properties and applications. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the different types of nanomaterials: (a) carbon-based, (b) metal-based, (c) dendrimers, and (d)
  • composites. Comment on their main properties and applications.
  • Carbon-based nanomaterials: Nanomaterials composed entirely of carbon atoms; examples: carbon nanotubes
  • (CNTs), graphene, fullerenes.
  • Metal-based nanomaterials: Nanomaterials composed of metals or metal oxides with at least one dimension in
  • the nanoscale; examples: Au, Ag, TiO₂, ZnO nanoparticles.

  • material properties; examples: polymer–clay nanocomposite, CNT–polymer composite.

questions.question: Discuss the principle of AFM. Evaluate its importance in the characterization of nanomaterials. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the principle of AFM. Evaluate its importance in the characterization of nanomaterials.
  • The principle of Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) is based on scanning a sharp tip on a flexible cantilever over a surface and
  • detecting the intermolecular forces between the tip and the sample. As the tip scans, it experiences forces (attractive or re pulsive)
  • that cause the cantilever to bend or change its oscillation. This deflection is detected by a laser beam that reflects off th e back of the
  • cantilever onto a position-sensitive photodiode, which translates the movement into a 3D image of the sample's surface topography.
  • AFM can image surfaces at the nanometer and even atomic scale, offering exceptional detail. Unlike many microscopes, AFM
  • provides true 3D topographical maps of the sample surface. AFM can operate in air, vacuum, or liquid, making it suitable for both
  • biological and material samples.
  • (Principle of AFM- 4 marks; Importance of AFM - any 3 points - 3 marks)

questions.question: Compare the advantages of SEM and TEM. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Compare the advantages of SEM and TEM.
  • • SEM provides three-dimensional surface morphology with a large depth of field, whereas TEM provides
  • detailed internal structural information with much higher resolution.
  • • SEM can analyse bulk or thick specimens with relatively simple sample preparation, whereas TEM requires
  • ultrathin specimens for electron transmission.
  • • SEM is mainly used for studying surface topography and morphology, whereas TEM is used for analysing
  • crystal structure, lattice defects and nanoparticle size.
  • (Any 3 points of difference -7 marks.)

questions.question: Explain the importance of UV - Visible spectra and IR spectra in the characterization of nanomaterials / [CO2] [7x5 = 35]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of UV Visible spectra and IR spectra in the characterization of nanomaterials
  • UV-Vis spectroscopy helps find the size and concentration of nanomaterials by measuring light absorption. Nanoparticles like gold
  • and silver show a special feature called surface plasmon resonance (SPR), where free electrons resonate with electromagnetic
  • radiation, causing strong absorption peaks. SPR peaks in UV-Visible spectra reveal the size, shape, and stability of nanoparticles in
  • solution.
  • IR spectroscopy identifies the chemical bonds and groups on nanomaterial surfaces. It helps confirm if the nanomaterial conta ins
  • specific molecules or coating substances. IR gives information about how atoms in nanomaterials are bonded and changes during
  • reactions
  • (Relevant explanation, UV – 3.5 marks, IR – 3.5 marks)

questions.question: What is X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy. Explain its importance in nanotechnology. / [CO2] [7x5 = 35]
questions.solution_html:
• What is X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy. Explain its importance in nanotechnology.
  • Definition: X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) is a surface analytical technique based on the photoelectric
  • effect, in which X-rays eject electrons from a material to determine its surface composition.
  • Importance: XPS is used to determine the elemental composition, chemical/oxidation state and surface chemical
  • bonding of nanomaterials.
  • Applications: It is widely used for surface characterization, thin-film analysis , nanomaterial quality control , and
  • catalyst and semiconductor studies.
  • (Definition-3 marks, Importance/application-4 marks)
